claim: A recent experiment on zebrafish blastoderm morphogenesis showed that the viscosity (η) of a non-confluent embryonic tissue grows sharply until a critical cell packing fraction (ϕS).
source: A recent experiment on zebrafish blastoderm morphogenesis showed that the viscosity (η) of a non-confluent embryonic tissue grows sharply until a critical cell packing fraction (ϕS).
evidence: This claim references experimental observations from prior work on zebrafish blastoderm.

claim: The increase in η up to ϕS is similar to the behavior observed in several glass-forming materials.
source: The increase in η up to ϕS is similar to the behavior observed in several glass-forming materials, which suggests that the cell dynamics is sluggish or glass-like.
evidence: This claim draws a comparison to known behavior in glass-forming materials based on established knowledge.

claim: η is a constant above ϕS.
source: Surprisingly, η is a constant above ϕS.
evidence: This is stated as a surprising experimental observation.

claim: Polydispersity in the cell size and the propensity of the cells to deform results in the saturation of the available free area per cell beyond a critical packing fraction.
source: We show that polydispersity in the cell size, and the propensity of the cells to deform, results in the saturation of the available free area per cell beyond a critical packing fraction.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Saturation in the free space explains the viscosity plateau above ϕS.
source: Saturation in the free space not only explains the viscosity plateau above ϕS but also provides a relationship between equilibrium geometrical packing to the dramatic increase in the relaxation dynamics.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation derived from simulation results.

claim: Measurements of bulk properties have been interpreted by adapting concepts developed to describe phase transitions, glass transition, and active matter.
source: Measurements of bulk properties, such as viscosity and elastic modulus, and the dynamics of individual cells through imaging techniques, have been interpreted by adapting concepts developed to describe phase transitions (PTs), glass transition, and active matter (Shaebani et al., 2020; Marchetti et al., 2013; Kirkpatrick and Thirumalai, 2015; Bär et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: During embryo morphogenesis, material properties of the tissues change dramatically.
source: Several experiments have shown that during embryo morphogenesis, material properties of the tissues change dramatically (Morita et al., 2017; Mongera et al., 2018; Barriga et al., 2018; Petridou et al., 2019; Petridou et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental citations.

claim: A PT occurs during zebrafish blastoderm morphogenesis, which was analyzed using rigidity percolation theory.
source: Of relevance to our study is a remarkable finding that provided evidence that a PT occurs during zebrafish blastoderm morphogenesis, which was analyzed using rigidity percolation theory (Petridou et al., 2021; Jacobs and Thorpe, 1995; Jacobs and Thorpe, 1996; Jacobs and Hendrickson, 1997).
evidence: This claim references experimental findings and theoretical analysis from cited work.

claim: Change in η is correlated with cell connectivity (⟨C⟩), rising sharply over a narrow range of ⟨C⟩.
source: It was found that change in η is correlated with cell connectivity (⟨C⟩), rising sharply over a narrow range of ⟨C⟩.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the cited work.

claim: A single geometrical quantity, the cell–cell contact topology controls both the rigidity PT and changes in η in this non-confluent tissue.
source: Surprisingly, a single geometrical quantity, the cell–cell contact topology controls both the rigidity PT and changes in η in this non-confluent tissue, thus linking equilibrium and transport properties.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental findings from cited work.

claim: η increases as a function of the cell packing fraction (ϕ) till ϕ≤0.87.
source: First, experiments (Sinha and Thirumalai, 2021) showed that η increases as a function of the cell packing fraction (ϕ) till ϕ≤0.87.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from cited work.

claim: The dependence of η on ϕ follows the well-known Vogel–Fulcher–Tammann (VFT) law.
source: The dependence of η on ϕ follows the well-known Vogel–Fulcher–Tammann (VFT) law (Sinha and Thirumalai, 2021), which predicts that η grows monotonically with ϕ.
evidence: This is an analysis of experimental data using a known theoretical framework.

claim: For packing fractions ϕ≥ϕS≈0.90, η deviates from the VFT law and is independent of ϕ.
source: Surprisingly, for packing fractions, ϕ≥ϕS≈0.90, η deviates from the VFT law and is independent of ϕ, which cannot be explained using conventional theories for glasses (Berthier and Biroli, 2011; Kirkpatrick and Thirumalai, 2015).
evidence: This is an experimental observation that contradicts conventional theories.

claim: The experimental data was interpreted using equilibrium rigidity percolation theory for an embryonic tissue in which cells undergo random cell divisions.
source: Second, the experimental data (Petridou et al., 2021) was interpreted using equilibrium rigidity percolation theory (Jacobs and Thorpe, 1995; Jacobs and Thorpe, 1996; Jacobs and Hendrickson, 1997) for an embryonic tissue in which cells undergo random cell divisions.
evidence: This describes the theoretical framework used to interpret experimental data.

claim: The interactions between the cells are soft.
source: We show that the two conundrums (saturation of η at high packing fractions and the use of equilibrium statistical mechanics in a growing system to explain PT) may be rationalized by (i) assuming that the interactions between the cells are soft, and (ii) the cell sizes are highly heterogeneous (polydisperse), which is the case in zebrafish blastoderm.
evidence: This is an assumption made in the modeling approach.

claim: The cell sizes are highly heterogeneous (polydisperse) in zebrafish blastoderm.
source: We show that the two conundrums (saturation of η at high packing fractions and the use of equilibrium statistical mechanics in a growing system to explain PT) may be rationalized by (i) assuming that the interactions between the cells are soft, and (ii) the cell sizes are highly heterogeneous (polydisperse), which is the case in zebrafish blastoderm.
evidence: This is an observation about zebrafish blastoderm supported by experimental data.

claim: The calculated effective viscosity η̄ for the polydisperse cell system shows that for ϕ≤ϕS≈0.90 the increase in viscosity follows the VFT law.
source: The central results of our study are (i) the calculated effective viscosity η¯ (for details see, Appendix 6, 'Dynamical changes in local packing fraction cause jammed cells to move'), for the polydisperse cell system, shows that for ϕ≤ϕS≈0.90 the increase in viscosity follows the VFT law.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the simulations.

claim: η is essentially independent of ϕ at high (≥ϕS) packing fractions in simulations.
source: Just as in experiments, η is essentially independent of ϕ at high (≥ϕS) packing fractions.
evidence: This is a simulation result that matches experimental observations.

claim: The unusual dependence of η at ϕ≥ϕS is quantitatively explained using the notion of available free area fraction (ϕfree).
source: (ii) The unusual dependence of η at ϕ≥ϕS is quantitatively explained using the notion of available free area fraction (ϕfree), which is the net void space that can be explored by the cells when they are jammed.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation derived from simulation analysis.

claim: ϕfree decreases with increasing packing fraction (ϕ) until ϕS.
source: Indeed, we find that ϕfree decreases with increasing packing fraction (ϕ) until ϕS.
evidence: This is a finding from simulation data analysis.

claim: When ϕ exceeds ϕS, the free area ϕfree saturates because the soft cells can overlap with each other.
source: The simulations show that when ϕ exceeds ϕS, the free area ϕfree saturates because the soft cells (characterized by 'soft deformable disks') can overlap with each other, resulting in the collective dynamics of cells becoming independent of ϕ for ϕ≥ϕS.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on simulation observations.

claim: Cells whose sizes are comparable to the available free area move almost like a particle in a liquid.
source: (iii) Cells whose sizes are comparable to the available free area move almost like a particle in a liquid.
evidence: This is an interpretation of simulation observations.

claim: The motility of small-sized cells facilitates adjacent cells to move through multi-cell rearrangement even in a highly jammed environment.
source: The motility of small-sized cells facilitates adjacent cells to move through multi-cell rearrangement even in a highly jammed environment.
evidence: This is a mechanism observed in simulations.

claim: The facilitation mechanism allows large cells to move with low mobility.
source: The facilitation mechanism, invoked in glassy systems (Biroli and Garrahan, 2013), allows large cells to move with low mobility.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on simulation observations and concepts from glass physics.

claim: The relaxation time does not depend on the waiting time for measurements even in the regime where viscosity saturates.
source: (iv) We find that the relaxation time does not depend on the waiting time for measurements even in the regime where viscosity saturates.
evidence: This is a finding from simulation analysis testing for aging effects.

claim: There is no evidence of aging even in the regime where viscosity saturates.
source: In other words, there is no evidence of aging even in the regime where viscosity saturates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the waiting time analysis.

claim: The tissue exhibits ergodic behavior at all densities.
source: Strikingly, the tissue exhibits ergodic (Thirumalai et al., 1989) behavior at all densities.
evidence: This is a conclusion from simulation analysis with a citation to the concept of ergodicity.

claim: The cell-based simulations may be described using equilibrium statistical mechanics.
source: The cell-based simulations, which reproduce the salient experimental features, may be described using equilibrium statistical mechanics, thus providing credence to the use of cell contact mechanics to describe both rigidity PT and dynamics in an evolving non-confluent tissue (Petridou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: There is considerable dispersion in cell sizes in zebrafish blastoderm.
source: A 2D section of zebrafish blastoderm (Figure 1B) shows that there is considerable dispersion in cell sizes.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental images.

claim: η increases sharply over a narrow ϕ range and saturates when ϕ exceeds ϕS≈0.90.
source: Figure 1C shows that η increases sharply over a narrow ϕ range and saturates when ϕ exceeds ϕS≈0.90.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data plot.

claim: A mono-disperse system in which all the cells have identical radius crystallizes.
source: To account for the results in Figure 1C, we first simulated a mono-disperse system in which all the cells have identical radius (R=8.5μm). Because the system crystallizes (Appendix 1—figure 1A and B), we concluded that the dynamics observed in experiments cannot be explained using this model.
evidence: This is a finding from simulations that ruled out a monodisperse model.

claim: A 1:1 binary mixture of cells with different radii gives glass-like behavior for all ϕ.
source: A 1:1 binary mixture of cells with different radii gives glass-like behavior for all ϕ, with the relaxation time τα as well as the effective viscosity η¯ (defined in Equation 1) following the VFT behavior (see Appendix 2).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations of a binary mixture model.

claim: In zebrafish, there is a great dispersion in the cell sizes, which vary in a single tissue by a factor of ∼5–6.
source: In typical cell tissues, and zebrafish in particular, there is a great dispersion in the cell sizes, which vary in a single tissue by a factor of ∼5–6 (Petridou et al., 2021; Figure 1B, Appendix 1—figure 1D).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data with citation and figure references.

claim: The elastic forces characterizing cell–cell interactions are soft, which implies that the cells can overlap.
source: In addition, the elastic forces characterizing cell–cell interactions are soft, which implies that the cells can overlap, with rij−(Ri+Rj)<0 when they are jammed (Figure 1B, D).
evidence: This is a modeling assumption supported by experimental observations.

claim: Different sized cells are well mixed and do not phase separate.
source: A simulation snapshot (Figure 1D) for ϕ=0.93 shows that different sized cells are well mixed. In other words, the cells do not phase separate.
evidence: This is an observation from simulation snapshots.

claim: The polydisperse cell system exhibits liquid-like structure even at high ϕ.
source: The absence of peaks in g(r) beyond the second one suggests there is no long-range order. Thus, the polydisperse cell system exhibits liquid-like structure even at the high ϕ.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pair correlation function from simulations.

claim: A fit of the experimental data for η using the VFT relation in the range ϕ≤0.87 yields ϕ0≈0.95 and D≈0.51.
source: A fit of the experimental data for η using the VFT (Tammann and Hesse, 1926; Fulcher, 1925) relation in the range ϕ≤0.87 (Figure 1C) yields ϕ0≈0.95 and D≈0.51 (Sinha and Thirumalai, 2021).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting experimental data.

claim: The value of ϕ0 obtained from simulations (ϕ0∼0.95) is close to ϕ0∼0.94 extracted by fitting the experimental data to the VFT equation.
source: The value of ϕ0 obtained from simulations, ϕ0∼0.95, is close to ϕ0∼0.94 extracted by fitting the experimental data to the VFT equation.
evidence: This is a comparison between simulation and experimental results.

claim: The dynamics for ϕ≤ϕS resembles the behavior expected for glass-forming systems.
source: Thus, the dynamics for ϕ≤ϕS resembles the behavior expected for glass-forming systems.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the VFT behavior observed in simulations.

claim: The dependence of η on ϕ over the entire range may be understood using available free area picture with essentially a single parameter.
source: Remarkably, the dependence of η on ϕ over the entire range (VFT regime followed by a plateau) may be understood using available free area picture with essentially a single parameter, an idea that was proposed nearly 70 y ago.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the simulation results referencing historical concepts.

claim: PD and the ease of deformation of the cells that creates free area under high jamming conditions is the mechanism that explains viscosity saturation at high cell densities.
source: We discovered that PD as well as the ease of deformation of the cells that creates free area under high jamming conditions is the mechanism that explains viscosity saturation at high cell densities.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion from the simulations.

claim: The mechanism suggested here links equilibrium PT to dynamics during zebrafish development.
source: The mechanism suggested here is an important step that links equilibrium PT to dynamics during zebrafish development (Hannezo and Heisenberg, 2022).
evidence: This is a broader implication of the findings with a citation.

claim: Preliminary simulations in three dimensions with reduced PD show that τα saturates at high-volume fractions.
source: We performed preliminary simulations in three dimensions with considerably reduced PD and calculated the dependence of relaxation time (τα) as a function of ϕ. The results show that τα does indeed saturate at high-volume fractions.
evidence: This is a finding from preliminary 3D simulations.

claim: Realistic values of adhesion strength would not significantly alter the forces between cells.
source: We do think that realistic values of adhesion strength would not significantly alter the forces between cells (Malmi-Kakkada et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation about the effect of adhesion with a citation.

claim: The physics of the dynamics in glass-forming materials does not change in systems with and without attractive forces.
source: Furthermore, the physics of the dynamics in glass-forming materials does not change in systems with and without attractive forces (Kirkpatrick and Thirumalai, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about glass-forming materials with a citation.

claim: Universal behavior, such as VFT relation, is valid for a broad class of unrelated materials.
source: Universal behavior, such as VFT relation, is valid for a broad class of unrelated materials (see Figure 1 in Angell, 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge about universal behavior in materials with a citation.

claim: Changing the adhesion strength would change ϕS without qualitatively altering the dependence of η on ϕ.
source: In our case, we expect that changing the adhesion strength, within a reasonable range, would change ϕS without qualitatively altering the dependence of η on ϕ.
evidence: This is a speculation about the effect of adhesion on the results.

claim: The calculation of viscosity using linear response theory and the link to free area quantitatively explain the simulation results and experimental data.
source: We find it surprising that the calculation of viscosity using linear response theory (valid for systems close to equilibrium) and the link to free area quantitatively explain the simulation results and by implication the experimental data for a living and growing tissue.
evidence: This is a reflection on the theoretical approach and its success.

claim: The calculation of free area of the cells is based on the geometrical effects of packing, which is determined by cell-to-cell contact topology.
source: The calculation of free area of the cells is based on the geometrical effects of packing, which in turn is determined by cell-to-cell contact topology.
evidence: This explains the basis for the free area calculation.

claim: Equilibrium PTs are related to a steep increase in viscosity as the packing fraction changes over a narrow range.
source: These considerations, which are firmly established here, explain why equilibrium PTs are related to a steep increase in viscosity (Kirkpatrick and Thirumalai, 2015) as the packing fraction changes over a narrow range.
evidence: This is a theoretical connection established by the work with a citation.

claim: The absence of aging suggests that cell divisions must be essentially independent, allowing the cells to reach local equilibrium.
source: The absence of aging suggests that, although a large number of cell divisions occur, they must be essentially independent, thus allowing the cells to reach local equilibrium.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the aging analysis results.

claim: Cell division was not explicitly included in the simulations because the time scales over which cell division induced local stresses relax are short compared to cell division time.
source: We did not explicitly include cell division in the simulations. This is physically reasonable because in the experiments (Petridou et al., 2021) the time scales over which cell division induced local stresses relax are short compared to cell division time.
evidence: This justifies a modeling choice based on experimental observations.

claim: Local equilibrium is established in between random cell division events.
source: Thus, local equilibrium is established in between random cell division events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time scale argument.

claim: Simulations were performed in 2D because experiments reported the dependence of viscosity as a function of area fraction.
source: We performed simulations in 2D because experiments reported the dependence of viscosity as a function of area fraction.
evidence: This justifies the choice of 2D simulations based on experimental measurements.

claim: Cells are modeled as soft deformable disks interacting via short-ranged forces.
source: In our model, cells are modeled as soft deformable disks (Matoz-Fernandez et al., 2017; Drasdo and Höhme, 2005; Schaller and Meyer-Hermann, 2005; Malmi-Kakkada et al., 2018) interacting via short-ranged forces.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach with citations to prior work.

claim: An active force arising from self-propulsion mobility (µ) is included as a proxy for the intrinsically generated forces within a cell.
source: In addition to the repulsive Hertz force, we include an active force arising from self-propulsion mobility (µ), which is a proxy for the intrinsically generated forces within a cell.
evidence: This describes a component of the model.

claim: The stress relaxation is clearly non-exponential, decaying to zero in two steps.
source: The time dependence of ⟨Pμν(t)Pμν(0)⟩, normalized by ⟨Pμν(0)2⟩, for different values of ϕ (Figure 7A and B) shows that the stress relaxation is clearly non-exponential, decaying to zero in two steps.
evidence: This is an observation from the stress correlation function analysis.

claim: The dynamics become sluggish as ϕ increases.
source: From Figure 2B and C, which show Fs(q,t) as a function of t for various ϕ, it is clear that the dynamics become sluggish as ϕ increases.
evidence: This is an observation from the self-intermediate scattering function.

claim: The relaxation profiles exhibit a two-step decay with a plateau in the intermediate time scales.
source: The relaxation profiles exhibit a two-step decay with a plateau in the intermediate time scales.
evidence: This describes the shape of the relaxation curves.

claim: The dynamics continues to slow down dramatically until ϕ≤0.90.
source: The dynamics continues to slow down dramatically until ϕ≤0.90.
evidence: This is an observation from the relaxation time analysis.

claim: The increase in the duration of the plateau in Fs(q,t) ceases when ϕ exceeds ≈0.90.
source: Surprisingly, the increase in the duration of the plateau in Fs(q,t) ceases when ϕ exceeds ≈0.90 (Figure 2C), a puzzling finding that is also reflected in the dependence of τα on ϕ in Figure 2D.
evidence: This is an observation from the self-intermediate scattering function.

claim: τα is nearly a constant when ϕ exceeds 0.90.
source: However, the simulations show that τα is nearly a constant when ϕ exceeds 0.90.
evidence: This is a finding from the relaxation time analysis.

claim: The behavior in Figure 2D differs from the dependence of τα on ϕ for 2D monodisperse polymer rings.
source: We should note that the behavior in Figure 2D differs from the dependence of τα on ϕ for 2D monodisperse polymer rings, used as a model for soft colloids. Simulations (Gnan and Zaccarelli, 2019) showed τα increases till a critical ϕS but it decreases substantially beyond ϕS with no saturation.
evidence: This is a comparison to other systems with a citation.

claim: τα changes by nearly eight orders of magnitude as a function of cell radius Ri.
source: Plot of τα as a function of the radius of cells Ri (Figure 3A) shows nearly eight orders of magnitude change.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of individual cell dynamics.

claim: τα increases for large-sized cells.
source: That τα should increase for large-sized cells (see the data beyond the vertical dashed line in Figure 3A) is not unexpected.
evidence: This is an expected observation from the cell size analysis.

claim: The relaxation times for cells with Ri<4.25μm are relatively short even though the system as a whole is jammed.
source: However, even when cell sizes increase beyond Ri=4.25μm, the dispersion in τα is substantial, especially when ϕ exceeds ϕS. The relaxation times for cells with Ri<4.25μm are relatively short even though the system as a whole is jammed.
evidence: This is an observation from the cell size-dependent relaxation analysis.

claim: For ϕ≥0.90, τα for small-sized cells have a weak dependence on ϕ.
source: For ϕ≥0.90, τα for small-sized cells have a weak dependence on ϕ.
evidence: This is an observation from the cell size-dependent relaxation analysis.

claim: The smaller-sized cells have the largest ⟨Afree⟩≈50μm2≈πRS2(RS≈4μm).
source: In what follows, we interpret these results in terms of available free area ⟨Afree⟩ for cells. The smaller-sized cells have the largest ⟨Afree⟩≈50μm2≈πRS2(RS≈4μm) (RS is the radius of the small cell).
evidence: This is a quantitative interpretation of the free area for small cells.

claim: The effect of jamming on the dramatic increase in τα occurs near Ri≈4.5μm, which is comparable to the length scale of short-range interactions.
source: The effect of jamming on the dramatic increase in τα occurs near Ri≈4.5μm, which is comparable to the length scale of short-range interactions.
evidence: This is an observation linking cell size to interaction length scales.

claim: At higher packing fractions, even cells of similar sizes show substantial variations in τα, which change by almost 3–4 orders of magnitude.
source: However, at higher packing fractions, even cells of similar sizes show substantial variations in τα, which change by almost 3–4 orders of magnitude (see the data around the vertical dashed line for ϕ≥0.915 in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation of heterogeneity in dynamics at high packing fractions.

claim: Large variations in τα are a consequence of large variations in the local density.
source: This is a consequence of large variations in the local density (Appendix 6—figure 1).
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed heterogeneity with a figure reference.

claim: Some similar-sized cells are trapped in the jammed environment, whereas others are in less crowded regions.
source: Some of the similar-sized cells are trapped in the jammed environment, whereas others are in less crowded regions (see Appendix 6—figure 1).
evidence: This describes spatial heterogeneity in the system.

claim: The spread in τα increases dramatically for ϕ>ϕS (≈0.90) and effectively overlap with each other.
source: The spread in τα increases dramatically for ϕ>ϕS (≈0.90) and effectively overlap with each other.
evidence: This is an observation from the histogram analysis.

claim: There are cells (typically with small sizes) that move faster even in a highly jammed environment.
source: There are cells (typically with small sizes) that move faster even in a highly jammed environment (see Appendix 5—figures 1C and 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation videos and analysis.

claim: The motions of the fast-moving cells change the local environment, which effectively facilitates the bigger cells to move in a crowded environment.
source: The motions of the fast-moving cells change the local environment, which effectively facilitates the bigger cells to move in a crowded environment (see Appendix 5—figures 1D and 2, Video 1 (ϕ=0.92>ϕS) and Video 2 (ϕ=0.90=ϕS)).
evidence: This describes the facilitation mechanism observed in simulations.

claim: For ϕ=0.85<ϕS, small- and large-sized cells move without hindrance because of adequate availability of free area.
source: In contrast, for ϕ=0.85<ϕS, small- and large-sized cells move without hindrance because of adequate availability of free area (Video 3).
evidence: This is an observation from simulation videos at lower packing fractions.

claim: The dependence of τα on ϕ for ϕ≤ϕS implies that the polydisperse cell systems behave as a soft glass in this regime.
source: The dependence of τα on ϕ for ϕ≤ϕS (Figure 2D) implies that the polydisperse cell systems behave as a soft glass in this regime.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relaxation time behavior.

claim: The prediction P(ln(τα))∼exp[−c(ln(τα/τ0))2] is valid in the polydisperse cell system for ϕ≤ϕS.
source: Remarkably, we found that this prediction is valid in the polydisperse cell system (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding that validates a theoretical prediction.

claim: Above ϕS the predicted relation P(ln(τα))∼exp[−c(ln(τα/τ0))2] is not satisfied.
source: However, above ϕS the predicted relation is not satisfied (see Figure 3D).
evidence: This shows a deviation from the theoretical prediction at high packing fractions.

claim: In a hard disk system, the free area would decrease monotonically with ϕ until it is fully jammed at the close packing fraction (∼0.84).
source: In a hard disk system, one would expect that the free area would decrease monotonically with ϕ until it is fully jammed at the close packing fraction (∼0.84; Drocco et al., 2005; Reichhardt and Reichhardt, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to hard disk systems with citations.

claim: Because the cells are modeled as soft deformable disks, they could overlap with each other even when fully jammed.
source: Because the cells are modeled as soft deformable disks, they could overlap with each other even when fully jammed.
evidence: This is a consequence of the modeling choice.

claim: The region where cells overlap creates free area in the immediate neighborhood.
source: Therefore, the region where cells overlap creates free area in the immediate neighborhood.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation for free area creation.

claim: The width in P(hij) increases with ϕ, and the peak shifts to higher values of hij.
source: The width in P(hij) increases with ϕ, and the peak shifts to higher values of hij (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the overlap distribution analysis.

claim: The mean ⟨hij⟩ increases with ϕ.
source: The mean, ⟨hij⟩, increases with ϕ (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the overlap analysis.

claim: Even if the cells are highly jammed at ϕ≈ϕS, free area is available because of an increase in the overlap between cells.
source: Thus, even if the cells are highly jammed at ϕ≈ϕS, free area is available because of an increase in the overlap between cells (see Figure 5).
evidence: This is a key mechanistic conclusion from the overlap and free area analysis.

claim: When ϕ exceeds ϕS, the mobility of small-sized cells facilitates the larger cells to move, as is assumed in the free volume theory of polymer glasses.
source: When ϕ exceeds ϕS, the mobility of small-sized cells facilitates the larger cells to move, as is assumed in the free volume theory of polymer glasses (Cohen and Turnbull, 1959; Turnbull and Cohen, 1961; Turnbull and Cohen, 1970; Falk et al., 2020).
evidence: This connects the simulation observations to free volume theory with citations.

claim: As a result of the motion of small cells, a void is temporarily created, which allows other (possibly large) cells to move.
source: As a result of the motion of small cells, a void is temporarily created, which allows other (possibly large) cells to move.
evidence: This describes the facilitation mechanism.

claim: If hij increases, the available space for nearby cells would also increase.
source: In addition to the release of space, the cells can also interpenetrate (Figure 4A and B). If hij increases, as is the case when the extent of compression increases (Figure 4A), the available space for nearby cells would also increase.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of cell overlap.

claim: The combined effect of PD and cell–cell overlap creates, via the self-propulsion of cells, additional free area that drives larger cells to move even under jammed conditions.
source: These arguments suggest that the combined effect of PD and cell–cell overlap creates, via the self-propulsion of cells, additional free area that drives larger cells to move even under jammed conditions.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion combining multiple effects.

claim: As ϕ increases, the distribution of Voronoi cell size shifts toward lower values.
source: As ϕ increases, the distribution shifts toward lower Voronoi cell size ⟨A⟩.
evidence: This is an observation from the Voronoi analysis.

claim: The mean Voronoi cell size ⟨A⟩ decreases as ϕ is increased.
source: The mean Voronoi cell size ⟨A⟩ as a function of ϕ in Figure 5C shows ⟨A⟩ decreases as ϕ is increased.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the Voronoi analysis.

claim: As cells interpenetrate, the Voronoi cell size will be smaller than the actual cell size in many instances.
source: As cells interpenetrate, the Voronoi cell size will be smaller than the actual cell size (πRi2) in many instances (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from the Voronoi tessellation.

claim: The value of Afree could be negative if the overlap between neighboring cells is substantial.
source: The value of Afree could be negative if the overlap between neighboring cells is substantial; Afree is positive only when the Voronoi cell size is greater than the actual cell size.
evidence: This defines the meaning of negative and positive free area.

claim: The histograms of Afree for all the packing fractions saturate beyond ϕ=0.90.
source: The histograms of Afree for all the packing fractions in Figure 5D show that the distributions saturate beyond ϕ=0.90.
evidence: This is an observation from the free area distribution analysis.

claim: All the distributions have a substantial region in which Afree is negative.
source: All the distributions have a substantial region in which Afree is negative.
evidence: This is an observation from the free area distributions.

claim: The negative value of Afree increases with increasing ϕ, which implies that the amount of interpenetration between cells increases.
source: The negative value of Afree increases with increasing ϕ, which implies that the amount of interpenetration between cells increases.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the free area distribution.

claim: Because of the overlap between the cells, the available free area fraction ϕfree is higher than the expected free area fraction (1.0−ϕ) for all ϕ.
source: Because of the overlap between the cells, the available free area fraction ϕfree is higher than the expected free area fraction (1.0−ϕ) for all ϕ.
evidence: This is a consequence of cell overlap on the free area calculation.

claim: ϕfree decreases with ϕ until ϕ=0.90, and then it saturates near a value ϕfree≈0.22.
source: The calculated ϕfree, plotted as a function of ϕ in Figure 5E, shows that ϕfree decreases with ϕ until ϕ=0.90, and then it saturates near a value ϕfree≈0.22 (see the right panel in Figure 5E).
evidence: This is the key quantitative finding about free area saturation.

claim: The saturation in η̄ as a function of ϕ is explained by the free area picture.
source: Thus, the saturation in η¯ as a function of ϕ is explained by the free area picture, which arises due to combined effect of the size variations and the ability of cells to overlap.
evidence: This is the main conclusion linking free area to viscosity saturation.

claim: Relaxation time τα in nearly monodisperse microgel PNiPAM was found to depend only weakly on the volume fraction if ϕV exceeds a critical value.
source: Relaxation time, τα, measured using dynamic light scattering, in nearly monodisperse microgel poly(N- isopropylacrylamide) (PNiPAM) (Philippe et al., 2018) was found to depend only weakly on the volume fraction (3D), if ϕV exceeds a critical value.
evidence: This is a comparison to experimental observations in another system with a citation.

claim: It was suggested that the near saturation of τα at high ϕV in PNiPAM is due to aging.
source: It was suggested that the near saturation of τα at high ϕV is due to aging, which is a non-equilibrium effect.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work about the PNiPAM system.

claim: If saturation in viscosity and relaxation time in the embryonic tissue at high ϕ is due to aging, then τα should increase sharply as the waiting time τω is lengthened.
source: If saturation in viscosity and relaxation time in the embryonic tissue at high ϕ is due to aging, then τα should increase sharply as the waiting time, τω, is lengthened.
evidence: This is a logical prediction to test the aging hypothesis.

claim: There is literally no change in Fs(q,t+τω) over the entire range of τω tested.
source: To test the effect of τω on τα, we calculated the self-intermediate scattering function Fs(q,t+τω) as a function of t by varying τω over three orders of magnitude at ϕ=0.92 (Figure 6A). There is literally no change in Fs(q,t+τω) over the entire range of τω.
evidence: This is a finding from the waiting time analysis.

claim: τα extracted from Fs(q,t+τω) is independent of τω.
source: We conclude that, τα, extracted from Fs(q,t+τω) is independent of τω.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the waiting time analysis.

claim: The variations in τα with respect to τω are significantly smaller than the errors in the simulation.
source: The variations in τα (Figure 6B), with respect to τω, are significantly smaller than the errors in the simulation.
evidence: This quantifies the lack of aging effect.

claim: The saturation in η or τα when ϕ>ϕS is not a consequence of aging.
source: Thus, the saturation in η or τα when ϕ>ϕS is not a consequence of aging.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the aging analysis.

claim: Although active forces drive the dynamics of the cells, the cell collectives can be treated as being near equilibrium.
source: There are two implications related to the absence of aging in the dynamics of the non-confluent embryonic tissues. (i) Although active forces drive the dynamics of the cells, as they presumably do in reality, the cell collectives can be treated as being near equilibrium, justifying the use of Green–Kubo relation to calculate η.
evidence: This is an implication of the absence of aging.

claim: The absence of significant non-equilibrium effects justifies the use of equilibrium rigidity percolation theory to analyze the experimental data.
source: (ii) Parenthetically, we note that the absence of significant non-equilibrium effects, even though zebrafish is a living system, further justifies the use of equilibrium rigidity percolation theory to analyze the experimental data (Petridou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is another implication of the absence of aging with a citation.

claim: Extensive computer simulations of a 2D dense tissue using a particle-based model have successfully reproduced the dynamical behavior observed in the blastoderm tissue of zebrafish.
source: Extensive computer simulations of a 2D dense tissue using a particle-based model of soft deformable cells with active self-propulsion have successfully reproduced the dynamical behavior observed in the blastoderm tissue of zebrafish.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main achievement.

claim: The dependence of viscosity and relaxation time before saturation is well fit by the VFT equation.
source: The dependence of viscosity (η) and relaxation time (τα) (before the saturation) is well fit by the VFT equation.
evidence: This is a summary of the fitting results.
